1.pericope_label: All the tribes come to Hebron, make a league with David and anoint him king over Israel

schools.summary: Henry presses the first of the three pleas into a mutual claim, that not only is David their bone and flesh but they are his, and he has as tender a concern for them as a man has for his own body, which Saul’s house had not; he sharpens the second to its edge, that when Saul was king he was but the cypher and David the figure; and on the third he glosses the shepherd language, that princes are to feed their people, consulting the subjects’ benefit, feeding them and not fleecing them. On the league he notes that the terms were sworn and subscribed on both sides, David binding himself to protect them as judge in peace and captain in war, and makes the witness the point, that it was a league before the Lord. From the three anointings he draws that David’s advances were gradual, so that his faith might be tried and experience gained, his kingdom thus typifying a greater one that was to come to its height by degrees. On the thirty years he observes that at that age the Levites were first appointed to begin their administration, that about that age the Son of David entered on his public ministry, and that then men come to their full maturity of judgment.

Gill has the tribes send ambassadors first, who report their reception, after which the elders come in person; he dates the embassy soon after the deaths of Abner and Ishbosheth, from any hand in which David had sufficiently cleared himself. He makes the thirty years the age at which David began to reign over Judah, the same age as his antitype when he entered on his public ministry, and reckons from the seven years and six months at Hebron that David was near thirty-eight when the elders came to him.

Ellicott alone notices that the divine promise the tribes quote is nowhere on record, the exact language not being found in the history, and offers two accounts of it: either a summary of communications made to David, as with words given earlier to Abner, or some unrecorded saying of a prophet. He enlarges the assembly from the elders to the great bodies of warriors listed in Chronicles, observes that the men of Judah, over whom David was already king, joined it, and notes the Levites present under Jehoiada with Zadok appearing only as a conspicuous member of that family. He warns that it would be an anachronism to read the league as a constitutional monarchy, but allows it may have covered particular matters, such as leading them against their enemies, sparing the remnant of Saul’s house, and not showing the partiality Saul had shown to men of his own tribe. From the thirty years he works outward, setting the combat with Goliath some ten or twelve years back, proving that the greater part of Saul’s reign is treated very briefly, and making David seventy at his death; and on the odd six months he observes that the sacred historians either dropped such fractions or counted them as whole years, an indefiniteness very marked in the parallel narratives of the two kingdoms. Keil and Delitzsch take the elders as the more exact definition of the tribes, and add that Chronicles supplies the words according to the word of the Lord through Samuel, so that the old command to anoint David found its complete fulfilment here.

Clarke numbers the three pleas plainly: David was their own countryman, he had been their general under Saul and had always led them to victory, and God had appointed him to govern and protect the people. He marks the anointing as the third, David having now taken the whole kingdom. Wesley takes the shepherd word as an admonition, that David was not made king to advance his own glory but for the good of his people, whom he ought to rule with all tenderness and watch over with all diligence; and he puts the league as mutual obligation, David to rule by God’s laws and the people to obey.

outliers.claim: Alone in observing that the divine promise the tribes cite is not found anywhere in the record.
Alone in turning the shepherd language into a rule of government, that princes are to feed their people and not fleece them.
Alone in reckoning David’s age at the second anointing, near thirty-eight, from the length of the Hebron reign.

6.pericope_label: The Jebusites taunt David with the blind and the lame; he takes the stronghold of Zion and dwells there

schools.summary: Henry offers two answers to the taunt and prefers neither outright: either the Jebusites confided in their gods, which David in contempt called the blind and the lame, for they have eyes and see not, feet and walk not — some thinking these were images of brass set in a recess of the fort and entrusted with its custody, idols they called their strongholds — or else in fortifications they thought so impregnable that the maimed could hold them. On the proverb he has the Jebusites say it first, meaning that if their images could not protect them they would never again trust their palladium, and David, having taken the fort, say it after them, that images which could not protect their worshippers should have no place there more. Watching David prosper from Millo inward, he adds that those who grow great must ascribe it to God’s presence.

Gill notes that David could not attempt a city partly belonging to Benjamin until Benjamin with the rest had made him king, and describes the stronghold as a fortress outside the city and separate from it, the taking of which would facilitate the taking of the rest.

Ellicott corrects the rendering of the taunt to Thou shalt not come hither, but the blind and the lame shall keep thee off, making it a boast rather than a condition. On the second verse he finds the sense obscured both by the Hebrew construction and by the word rendered gutter, which occurs elsewhere only once, as waterspouts, and likeliest means the watercourses about the precipices of Zion; a very slight change in the Masoretic vowels turns getteth into hurl, so that the order reads, whosoever smites the Jebusites, let him hurl the lame and the blind down the precipice, David throwing their own phrase back at them. That they are hated of his soul shows no quarter was to be given, these Canaanites lying under the old ban. He observes that the words he shall be chief and captain are not in the Hebrew here but stand in Chronicles, and draws from them a consequence no one else does: David promised the command of his army to whoever led the forlorn hope, Joab did it, and that helps explain the restraint David afterwards felt towards him. Keil and Delitzsch ground the Jebusite boast in the site, a mountain shut in by deep valleys on three sides, reach the same rendering of the hurling, derive Zion from a root meaning dry, and explain the choice of it as naturally strong and conveniently placed on the border of Benjamin and Judah.

Clarke declines the dispute and then supplies an emendation anyway. Scarcely a passage in the sacred oracles, he says, has puzzled commentators more; for his own part he thinks it not worth the labour spent on it, and will not encumber his pages with the discordant opinions of learned men; on the face of the text the Jebusites simply set the lame and blind on the walls to turn David’s attempt into ridicule, than which nothing could be more cutting to a warrior. He then prints Kennicott’s corrected text beside the English, which turns the taunt into a prediction that the blind and the lame shall drive David away, and promises the chief command to whoever reaches them through the subterranean passage. Wesley takes only the fortification sense of the taunt, supposing they set a parcel of blind and lame people, invalids or maimed soldiers, on the wall in contempt of David and his men; and he makes the proverb David’s own, ordained to keep up the memory of the exploit and of the Jebusites’ insolence, so that those once set to keep others out are now shut out themselves. He keeps the older rendering of scaling to the gutter at the top, noting that the missing clause is fitly supplied from Chronicles.

11.pericope_label: Hiram builds David a house; David perceives he is established for Israel’s sake, and takes more wives

schools.summary: Henry grants that the Jews were husbandmen and shepherds who did not much addict themselves to merchandise or manufactures, but turns the point: many have excelled in arts and sciences who were strangers to the covenants of promise, and David’s house was never the worse, nor the less fit to be dedicated to God, for being built by the sons of the stranger. On the establishing of the kingdom he notes that it stood with nothing to shake it and was exalted in the eyes of friends and enemies alike, and he makes the perceiving the heart of the verse, since many have God’s favour and do not perceive it, and so want the comfort of it, whereas to be exalted to it, established in it, and to perceive it, is happiness enough. Above all he owns the reason given: God did not make Israel his subjects for his sake, that he might be great and absolute, but made him their king for their sake, to lead and guide and protect them. On the wives he is blunt — shall we praise him for this? We praise him not, we justify him not, nor can we scarcely excuse him — though the patriarchs’ example might make him think there was no harm in it, and he might hope it would strengthen his interest by alliances; and he adds that all these wives did not keep him from coveting his neighbour’s, since men who have once broken the fence will wander.

Gill makes this Hiram the father of the Hiram of Solomon’s time, named Abibalus before he took the name Hiram, which became a common name of Tyre’s kings, and dates the city to a year before the fall of Troy. He reads David’s perceiving off his unbroken success in everything he set his hand to, and says plainly that the taking of more wives was not to his honour and contrary to the law of God.

Ellicott holds this Hiram the same man who was afterwards Solomon’s friend and works out the cost of saying so: since that Hiram was still living in the twenty-fourth year of Solomon’s reign, either he reigned some fifty-seven years or this embassy came well after the capture of Jerusalem. He rejects the thirty-four years Josephus quotes from Menander, since David was already in his house of cedar, before Solomon was born, when he purposed to build the temple, though he grants the later Huram’s father bore the same name. He infers from the Phoenician workmen that the Israelites had little architecture of their own, relying on them for this palace, for Solomon’s and for the temple; puts David’s perceiving as self-knowledge, that prosperity had not blinded him to his blessings coming to him as head of the theocracy; and says of the wives that he came perilously near a violation of the law without going the length of Solomon. Keil and Delitzsch treat Hiram simply as the ally of both kings, give the reason for the establishing as God’s having chosen Israel and promised to make it great, and make the wives a case of cultural capture, a large harem having been held from time immemorial part of an oriental court, so that David let custom seduce him past the prohibition.

Clarke calls Hiram a very friendly man and no doubt a believer in the true God, who assisted Solomon also in building the temple. On the wives he alone argues from nature: that dispensation permitted polygamy, but from the beginning it was not so, and since on average about fourteen males are born to thirteen females, polygamy is unnatural and could never have entered God’s original design. Wesley gives the reason for the establishing as that David might be a blessing to Israel and they be happy under his administration; and he reckons the wives among David’s miscarriages, expressly forbidden to a king, assigning the political motive of strengthening his interest by alliances, and adding in almost Henry’s words that all these did not keep him from coveting his neighbour’s wife, since men who have once broken the fence will wander.

17.pericope_label: Two Philistine invasions of the valley of Rephaim, broken at Baal-perazim and by the sound in the trees

schools.summary: Henry puts the Philistine calculation sharply, that he who under Saul had slain his ten thousands would be more formidable now he was king himself, and their error more sharply, that they considered not how David had the presence of God which Saul had forfeited; he reads the whole as the second psalm acted out, the heathen raging in vain. On the two enquiries he divides the question, his conscience asking whether he should go up and his prudence whether he would prosper: one would think the first needed no asking, since what was he made king for but to fight the Lord’s battles, but a good man loves to see God go before him. He alone finds a scruple in it, that though the Philistines were public enemies some had been his particular friends, Achish having sheltered him in his distress, so that he might rather have thought of making peace — to which the answer is that they are Israel’s enemies and he need not scruple. On the images he closes with Bishop Patrick’s antithesis, that when the ark fell into Philistine hands it consumed them, but when these images fell into the hands of Israel they could not save themselves from being consumed; and on the sound he allows that angels tread light, and that he who can walk on the clouds can walk on the tops of trees, though he also gives Bishop Patrick’s reading of the phrase as the hedge-row of the wood.

Gill lists the provocations together — the civil war ended, David strengthened, Jerusalem taken and Hiram befriended — and reports Kimchi’s view that David wrote the second psalm at this time. He notes that having prospered in the first battle David still would not engage again without the mind of God. On the sound he has the wind rustling the tops so as to resemble armies moving in the air, and reports that Jarchi and the Targum take it for angels sent to help David.

Ellicott explains the timing, that Philistine attention had been occupied with Abner and Ishbosheth, so that only the uniting of the old nation under their old foe alarmed them, and that the time their mustering took is what allowed David to take Jerusalem first. He warns that the name Baal-perazim has no reference to the heathen deity, and notes the victory was remembered centuries later as an instance of divine aid. On the trees he takes the baca-shrub as now generally understood, and notes that the word for the sound is used elsewhere of the Lord’s hosts marching. Keil and Delitzsch use the two enquiries polemically, as overthrowing Diestel’s assertion that the holy lot is not heard of after Saul’s death, and with it his inference that David valued it only to give definiteness to his command over his followers rather than from reverence. They add that Chronicles supplies the burning of the images, which the law prescribed; and they refuse both traditional renderings of the trees, the Greek pear-trees and the rabbinic mulberries, as uncertain, preferring an Arabic shrub of Mecca like the balsam, from a broken leaf of which flows a white sap like a tear, whence they suppose its name, from the root meaning to weep.

Clarke observes that since Saul fell the Philistines had held the principal places of Israel undisturbed, and now thought best to strike before David’s army grew too numerous. Wesley glosses Baal-perazim as the master of breaches and makes the naming an ascription to God, taking the simile of floods that break their banks and overturn all in their way; he gives Bishop Patrick’s antithesis about the ark and the images almost word for word as Henry has it, without naming its author; and on the sound he makes it work both ways at once, assuring David that God was coming and frightening the Philistines so that they never heard his army until it was upon them.
